claims.text: The initial HEA multilayers have relatively incoherent interfaces.
The transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep is uncontrolled in the initial multilayers.
CoCrFeNiTi can serve as a transition interlayer between HEA multilayers.
A deposited CoCrFeNiTi interlayer can be engineered to have a nanocrystalline structure.
The CoCrFeNiTi interlayer can be given lattice parameters optimized to match the adjacent HEA layers.
Atomic diffusion and dislocation glide may both be active during moderate-to-elevated-temperature constant-load creep testing.
A lattice-matched CoCrFeNiTi interlayer enhances interface coherency.
Enhanced interface coherency reduces interfacial defects and strain mismatch.
Reducing interfacial defects and lattice mismatch limits atomic diffusion across the interface.
Limiting interfacial diffusion shifts creep from a diffusion-dominated regime to a dislocation-mediated regime.
The CoCrFeNiTi transition layer delays the onset of diffusion-mediated creep.
The transition layer produces more pronounced dislocation activity than a multilayer without the interlayer.
The transition layer improves high-temperature creep resistance relative to a system without the interlayer.
Incoherent interfaces in conventional HEA multilayers cause an earlier transition to diffusion-mediated creep.
Conventional HEA multilayers without a tailored interlayer have poor creep resistance.
Very high temperatures may diminish the beneficial creep effect of the engineered interlayer.
Extreme stress levels overwhelmingly favor diffusion and may diminish the beneficial effect of the interlayer.
In-situ TEM and synchrotron XRD can jointly monitor interface structure and deformation mechanisms during creep.

contradictions.description: The proposed direction of transition is inconsistent: the hypothesis and mechanism describe a shift from diffusion-dominated to dislocation-mediated creep, whereas the baseline and predicted outcome frame the relevant temperature-dependent event as the onset of, or transition to, diffusion-mediated creep.

The boundary attributes overwhelming diffusion to extreme stress, while the predicted outcome associates enhanced deformation under the intervention with dislocation activity; the stress dependence and transition direction are not reconciled.
